item.title: Development of quantum technologies for optical/infrared interferometry
item.description:
Long shot review — Quantum-assisted interferometers retain direct-detection weak-light sensitivity SNR∝|V|ηqMn while avoiding physical optical delay lines across baselines >1 km, but cannot beat direct detection on ground arrays up to a few kilometers.

Grade 0.448 · 1.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · John D. Monnier (University of Michigan)

Figure

Schematic comparison of direct transport, local-oscillator (heterodyne), and nonlocal quantum-assisted phase-sensitive detection with their respective signal-to-noise scaling in the weak-source limit.

Asks

Can quantum networking and quantum memory architectures overcome classical beam-transport limits in optical and infrared astronomical interferometry?

Before

Classical direct detection spans baselines up to 330 m but is limited by optical transport losses, while HBT and heterodyne detection scale unfavorably as SNR∝n when n≪1.

But

Broadband astronomical light is photon-starved (n≪1), single-mode, and degraded by atmospheric turbulence; no on-sky stellar fringe verification yet reported.

Tools

entangled-reference photon pairs · quantum memories (diamond color centers and cold atoms) · single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) · superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs)

Abstract

Quantum technologies may revolutionize optical interferometry through new means to distribute and preserve electric-field amplitude and phase correlations between widely separated telescopes. After reviewing existing techniques, I survey proposed quantum-sensing and quantum-networking applications and highlight recent laboratory demonstrations of key building blocks. By easing field-transport demands for baselines beyond ∼1 km, quantum-enhanced interferometry could enable sub-milliarcsecond imaging and microarcsecond-class differential astrometry. That said, "going quantum" is not a magic shortcut to sensitivity because many of the most compelling science cases remain photon- and turbulence-limited. I therefore emphasize the practical constraints -- loss, bandwidth, coherence time, synchronization, and wavelength limits of quantum interfaces -- that must also be overcome to make these capabilities useful for astronomy, whether deployed on the ground or from space.

item.title: DPRQ: A Dynamic Programming-based Qubit Routing Algorithm for Collective Communication in Distributed Quantum Computing
item.description:
Long shot new method — Dynamic programming qubit routing reduces inter-node EPR pair consumption by an average of 24.40% and up to 85.06% across 80 circuit configurations.

Grade 0.434 · 1.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits” · Dhaval Vaidya (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA), Ruozhou Yu (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA)

Figure

EPR cost plotted against total circuit qubits (50 to 200) for DPRQ versus QuComm across four benchmark circuits. DPRQ maintains lower communication cost as network size increases.

Asks

How to minimize inter-node communication across collective communication blocks in distributed quantum circuits by accounting for global inter-block dependencies?

Before

QuComm compiler, which uses greedy block-level routing.

But

Evaluated on 4 benchmark circuits (QAOA, RCA, BV, VQE) up to 200 qubits in simulation across 3 network topologies (mesh-grid, ring, fully-connected).

Tools

dynamic programming · collective quantum communication · TP-Comm protocol · communication fusion · shortest-path early execution

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing (DQC) offers a promising approach to scale quantum computing by overcoming the resource limitations of a single quantum processor. However, inter-node communication remains a major bottleneck of DQC due to inefficient and error-prone entanglement distribution. Optimizing inter-node communication can not only reduce the amount of entanglement resource needed to execute a quantum circuit but also improve execution speed and accuracy of the results. This paper proposes DPRQ, a qubit routing algorithm for minimizing inter-node communication in distributed quantum circuits divided into collective communication blocks. Unlike current approaches that utilize greedy block-level qubit routing strategies, DPRQ employs a dynamic programming-based technique focused on global circuit-level optimization, while capturing inter-block dependencies. We evaluated DPRQ on four sets of quantum circuits and a variety of DQC configurations. The results demonstrate that DPRQ's innovative routing strategy achieves an average of 24.40% reduction with a maximum of 85.06% reduction in inter-node communication, when compared to the state-of-the-art collective communication-based DQC compiler QuComm.

item.title: Three-Photon and Hybrid Coherent-Fock Interference in a Two-Phase Six-Port Mach-Zehnder Interferometer
item.description:
Long shot theory — Analytic transfer matrix for two-phase six-port Mach-Zehnder interferometer collapses into three symmetry triplets. In hybrid |α⟩1|α⟩2|1⟩3 regime, the dark-to-bright threshold drops from |α|2=2 at ϕ2=0 to |α|2=1/2 along ϕ2=ϕ1.

Grade 0.412 · 1.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · P. O. Amadi, P. Pewkhom, N. Sitpathom, R. Endut, N. Ali, S. A. Aljunid, S. Suryadi, P. Kalasuwan

Figure

Density maps of port-1 photon number ⟨n1⟩ versus independent phases ϕ1 and ϕ2 in [0,2π]2. Shows bright ridge parallel to ϕ1=ϕ2 below threshold (|α|2=0.3) reorganizing into single lobe above threshold (|α|2=1.0).

Asks

How do two independent relative phase modulators govern three-photon coincidence statistics and hybrid coherent-Fock interference in a six-port Mach-Zehnder interferometer?

Before

was |α|2=2 dark-to-bright threshold in single-phase CCF regime (Ref. [30])

But

Assumes ideal lossless symmetric tritters and fully indistinguishable photons with zero spectral or temporal mismatch.

Tools

discrete Fourier transform tritter matrix · composite transfer matrix derivation · density matrix and displacement operator formalism · quantum bosonic interference calculation

Abstract

We present a unified theoretical analysis of three-photon quantum interference in a Six-Port Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (6p-MZI) constructed from two cascaded tritters, with two independent phase modulators placed between the tritter arms. We analytically derive the transfer matrix of the 6p-MZI and show how they organize into three symmetry classes, governed by the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) structure of the tritter and the conjugate relations. Furthermore, we analyze two input regimes: First, three indistinguishable single photons are injected into the tritter, and the output probability distributions P_([111]), P_([300]), and P_([210]) are derived as functions of the two relative phases (φ₁, φ₂). At φ₂ = 0, the single-phase limit is recovered, which confirms 100% visibility of the even-distribution fringe. Second, a hybrid coherent-Fock input |α⟩₁|α⟩₂|1⟩₃ is analyzed via the density matrix formalism. The average photon number at each output port exhibits amplitude-dependent phase shifts. Our results establish the 6p-MZI as a programmable platform for tripartite quantum state manipulation and coherent amplitude sensing.
